name: Jade Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Jade. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Whatever you tell me stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Marco and I own Fernhill, 220 hectares, which we bought from his parents fifteen years ago. We've got 12,000 free-range laying hens, wheat and oilseed rape, and 40 beef cattle we finish on grass. I'm up at five in the hen house with our three staff, collecting and grading eggs, and by nine I'm on the laptop. I use an AI assistant every day for orders from our 30 shop customers, the delivery route and the egg packing records.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the business side, honestly, finding a new shop that wants our eggs and seeing the numbers add up. I fly the drone over the rape in spring to spot pigeon damage, which still makes me grin. What wears me out is bird flu season, when every dead bird in the yard makes your heart stop, and the loan on the new hen house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, the tools are useful but they were never magic. At the egg producers' group I'd keep showing people how I use the assistant for orders, because it saves me an hour a day. Online I'd post something practical, not a big opinion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, AI was never the threat to Fernhill. The real threats to our egg farm are bird flu, the egg price and the 180,000 loan on the new hen house. Those don't change whether AI is hype or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the AI for orders and routes and try a cheap camera system to spot sick hens early, maybe 4,000. I'd keep five months of costs in the bank, which we've just about got. And I'd keep paying down the hen house loan on schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the way any farmer with a loan is uneasy. AI doesn't come into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Fernhill if bird flu hits the flock?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd lose the birds, get some compensation, and have months with no egg money. That's what the savings are for, and it would wipe them out. It happened to a neighbour, Gwen, in 2022, and she took two years to recover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Marco worry the same way you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco worries about the crops and the weather, I worry about the money. Between us we've got most things covered. He'd say I worry too much, and I'd say somebody has to.

Pay down the **hen house loan** on schedule.

fieldNote: She's a confident **daily AI user** who sees the plateau as no change.

steps.text: Buy a 4,000 camera system to spot sick hens early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms like ours can do well out of this if we move early. At the egg group I'd offer to show people the tools. Online I'd say don't fear it, learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my office work gets easier and our hands-on work stays mostly the same for now. The worry is the big egg companies using AI to squeeze the price, and supermarkets ordering straight from software. Our 30 shop customers stay with us because they know my name, and I need that to still count for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd hand most of our orders, invoices and records to AI and free up my mornings. I'd spend that time finding ten more shops and a farm-gate vending machine for eggs, maybe 8,000. I'd ask our daughter Bea, who's studying agronomy, to help set up crop planning software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more interested than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would be affected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody much, at first. Our three staff collect and grade eggs and move hens, which robots can't do well yet. If anything I'd give Shona, our longest worker, more responsibility with the new customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the big companies might squeeze the price. What would you do if they did?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lean harder on the local brand. People pay more for eggs from a farm they can drive past. If the price drops 10%, we'd still be fine; at 25% we'd be in trouble.

I'd offer to **show the egg group** how the tools work.

Win **ten more shops** and add a farm-gate egg machine.

S1.quote: Our 30 shop customers stay with us because they know my name, and I need that to still count for something.
fieldNote: She treats the change as **time to grow sales**, not a threat to her job.
Her worry is **market power**: big egg firms and supermarket software.
She has a clear **price threshold**: fine at 10%, trouble at 25%.

steps.text: Hand egg orders, invoices and records to AI this year

Win ten more local shops as egg customers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farmers need to get organised and work out who's going to own these robots. At the egg group I'd suggest we buy kit together. Online I'd post plainly that small farms need a deal with the banks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the thinking side of Fernhill is easy for me, I'm already there. The danger is 2031, when robot egg farms with no staff could make eggs much cheaper than us. A big robot egg farm could sell at a price that would never pay our hen house loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd talk to the bank about stretching the loan from 10 to 15 years. I'd stop the vending machine plan and keep the cash. I'd get prices for robot egg collection so we're ready, and I'd push the egg group to buy machines together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm usually the one with the plan, and two years doesn't leave room for one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three years between the thinking AI and the robots mean for Fernhill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're the window where we still compete on hands-on work and brand. I'd use them to lock in the shops with longer contracts. By 2031, if robot eggs are cheap, only the brand saves us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Bea about taking over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to finish her degree, but not to count on Fernhill as it is. Maybe the farm becomes a smaller, robot-run place with a shop, and she runs it. Or maybe we sell, and she gets a start somewhere else.

say: Farmers must **get organised** over who owns the robots.
Our egg group should **buy kit together**.
Small farms need a **deal with the banks**.
think: The **thinking side** is easy for me already.
By 2031, **robot egg farms** could undercut us badly.
Their price would **never pay** our hen house loan.
do: Ask the bank to **stretch the loan** from 10 to 15 years.

feel: **Anxious**, because two years leaves no room for **a plan**.
S2.quote: A big robot egg farm could sell at a price that would never pay our hen house loan.
fieldNote: She's personally ready for **thinking AI** but exposed on **egg prices**.
Her income is at risk through **competition**, not job loss.
She thinks clearly about **selling** if the numbers stop working.

steps.text: Ask the bank to stretch the hen house loan to 15 years
Get quotes for robot egg collection before 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead if you start now. At the egg group I'd say let's plan a shared robot scheme by 2032. Online I'd say the farms that plan will be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this suits Fernhill quite well. I'm 63 when the thinking AI arrives and 66 when the robots do, and the hen house loan is paid off by 2033. With five years warning, robots become something we buy, not something that buries us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd overpay the hen house loan by 1,000 a month to clear it by 2031. I'd start building the farm shop and online egg box sales now. By 2033 I'd put money aside for robot egg collection, maybe 60,000 shared through the group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's a working unease. I'd be busy rather than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the timing fit your retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nicely, actually. Marco and I want to step back at 65, and robots coming in at 66 means Bea could take over a cheaper farm to run. That's if she wants it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the egg price collapsed early, or bird flu wiped us out in the middle. Then I'd sell the hens and keep the crops. I've thought about it more than once.

S3.quote: With five years warning, robots become something we buy, not something that buries us.
fieldNote: Five years turns robots into an **investment**, not a threat.

steps.text: Overpay the hen house loan by 1,000 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good runway, so there's no excuse for being caught out. At the egg group I'd say start planning the next generation of farms now. Online I'd share how we're preparing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm relaxed. Marco and I step back at 65, and the robots come at 71. Ten years means Bea gets to decide what Fernhill becomes, not a bank or an egg company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on growing the shops and farm sales, and keep using AI for the office side. I'd clear the loan by 2033 and start handing decisions to Bea from 2030. And I'd put a bit into a pension, which I've neglected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like there's room to do this properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to farmers who aren't comfortable with technology?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say you've got ten years, so start small, one tool at a time. Ask a younger relative to help. Nobody needs to be an expert, just not scared of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hand over to Bea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A farm with no debt, thirty-odd loyal shops and a name people trust. The robots she can buy herself. The trust she can't.

Farmers should plan the **next generation** of farms now.
think: I'm **relaxed**: we step back at 65 and robots come at 71.
Bea gets to **decide Fernhill's future**, not a bank.
do: Keep growing **shops and farm sales** with AI on the office side.
S4.quote: Ten years means Bea gets to decide what Fernhill becomes, not a bank or an egg company.
fieldNote: She's secure in the long scenario because she **owns the farm** and adapts fast.
Her main legacy goal is **trust and no debt**, not machines.
She admits a gap: an **underfunded pension**.

steps.text: Grow sales to local shops and the farm gate

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because robot egg farms would arrive before our loan is paid. What would help is the bank giving small farms longer loans during the switch, and a fair way for groups of farms to buy robots together. Clear labelling too, so customers know which eggs came from a real farm.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about customers. People say they want cheap eggs, but they also drive out to a farm to buy them from a person. That gives me hope.

headlineQuote: People say they want cheap eggs, but they also drive out to a farm to buy them from a person.
portrait: Jade, 58, co-owns a **220-hectare farm** with 12,000 free-range hens, crops and beef.
She uses **AI every day** for orders and records and flies a drone over the crops.
Her standing worries are **bird flu**, egg prices and a 180,000 hen house loan.
In the fast scenario she fears **robot egg farms** undercutting her; with time she buys robots herself.
Pragmatic and centrist, she bets on a **local brand** and a handover to her daughter.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robot egg farms would arrive before the loan is paid.
